title: Initial revision of git, the information manager from hell
book_use: Chapter 1: anchors Git's first public commit to April 7 2005; eleven files; use the commit and original README language without implying later success was inevitable.

title: A Short History of Git
book_use: Chapter 1: Linux kernel moved to BitKeeper in 2002; the relationship broke down in 2005 and free-of-charge use was revoked; records the early design goals of speed, simple design, non-linear development, full distribution, and large-project efficiency.

title: GIT - the stupid content tracker (initial README)
book_use: Chapter 2: original object-database and current-directory-cache description; content-addressed object naming and the deliberately low-level initial design.

title: Git Internals - Git Objects
book_use: Chapter 2: blobs, trees, commits, tags, content-addressable storage and object relationships; explanatory secondary source for readers.

title: Git Branching - Branches in a Nutshell
book_use: Chapter 3: branches as lightweight movable pointers to commits and HEAD as the current branch reference; supports explanation of cheap branching without claiming other VCSs lacked branches.

title: Distributed Git - Distributed Workflows
book_use: Chapters 3 and 5: Git's distributed topology permits contributors and integrators to act as both nodes and hubs; use to separate Git's model from centralized forge habit.

title: A note from the maintainer
book_use: Chapter 4: identifies Junio C Hamano as current maintainer and documents mailing-list-centered development and integration practice; supports governance story without treating Git as leaderless.

title: Pull Requests 2.0
book_use: Chapters 6 and 7: GitHub says pull requests existed from launch and by 2010 were explicitly framed as living discussions and code review around proposed merges.

title: We Launched
book_use: Chapter 6: anchors GitHub's public launch to April 10 2008 and records launch-era features including comments on commits and network graphs; use as a concrete historical scene rather than a retrospective origin myth.

title: Only the beginning
book_use: Chapter 6: records GitHub's early growth from private beta in January 2008 to more than 50,000 public repositories by the start of 2009; supports the argument that a common social surface rapidly compressed project discovery and participation costs.

title: Microsoft completes GitHub acquisition
book_use: Chapter 6: anchors the completed Microsoft acquisition to October 26 2018 and supports the discussion of platform concentration without treating ownership as a change to Git's object model.

title: Status checks
book_use: Chapter 7: status checks attach automated validation results to commits and can be required before protected-branch merges.

title: About protected branches
book_use: Chapter 7: protected branches can require reviews, status checks, conversation resolution, signed commits, linear history, merge queues, and deployments; supports governance-layer discussion without treating these as Git primitives.

title: Git Virtual File System Architecture
book_use: Chapter 8: documents Microsoft's Windows-codebase scaling problem with millions of files and GVFS's strategy of virtualizing the working tree and downloading only content developers actually need; use as a concrete case of Git surviving by adding selective materialization layers.

title: About Git Large File Storage
book_use: Chapter 9: Git LFS stores a pointer in the Git repository while the large payload is stored separately; pointer includes SHA-256 object identity and size. Use as a concrete example of preserving Git coordination while externalizing heavy payloads.

title: Git LFS specification
book_use: Chapter 9: pointer files are canonical text records with version, SHA-256 oid and size; supports the distinction between versioning payload identity and storing payload bytes as ordinary Git blobs.

title: Announcing Git Large File Storage (LFS)
book_use: Chapter 9: anchors Git LFS's public announcement to April 8 2015 and records its explicit purpose of keeping small text pointers in Git while large binary payloads live on a remote server.

title: hash-function-transition
book_use: Chapters 10 and 18: SHA-256 repository transition goals, compatibility mappings and conversion across SHA-1 boundaries; supports migration as ecosystem namespace problem and distinguishes migration design from current defaults.

title: Announcing the first SHA1 collision
book_use: Chapter 10: anchors SHAttered to February 23 2017 and documents the first practical SHA-1 collision using two visually different PDFs with the same SHA-1 digest; use to show why generic SHA-1 collision resistance could no longer be treated as a distant theoretical concern.

title: SHA-1 collision detection on GitHub.com
book_use: Chapter 10: documents GitHub's March 2017 deployment of collision detection that rejects Git content showing evidence of collision attacks; supports the distinction between SHA-1's long-term unsuitability and Git-specific mitigations against known collision techniques.

title: git-commit-graph
book_use: Chapter 11: commit-graph is serialized auxiliary data for graph operations, including split graphs and changed-path support; illustrates derived acceleration structures rather than replacement of commit objects.

title: Scalar
book_use: Chapter 11: background maintenance, multi-pack-index coverage and commit-graph maintenance for large repositories; supports storage-engine evolution under stable Git commands.

title: git-merge
book_use: Chapter 12: three-way merge behavior, true merge parentage, conflict index stages, AUTO_MERGE under the default ort strategy, and the distinction between automatic combination and manual resolution.

title: git-rerere
book_use: Chapter 12: rerere records manual conflict resolutions and can reuse them when substantially the same conflict recurs; supports automation-as-memory without claiming it validates semantic correctness.

title: BreakingChanges
book_use: Chapters 13 and 18: Git 3.0 has no announced release date; tracks SHA-256 and reftable as defaults for new repositories, main as the default initial branch, staged Rust adoption culminating in mandatory Rust subject to downstream evaluation, safer bare-repository defaults, removal of long-deprecated features, and the safe.bareRepository threat model.

title: git-config
book_use: Chapters 13 and 14: current safe.directory ownership trust and safe.bareRepository configuration semantics plus signing formats, allowed signers, validity windows and revocation configuration; grounds both repository trust-boundary and signature trust-store discussion.

title: githooks
book_use: Chapter 13: hooks are executable programs invoked at defined Git events and can be relocated via core.hooksPath; supports execution-surface discussion without implying cloned repositories universally carry active hooks.

title: Git security vulnerability announced
book_use: Chapter 13: documents CVE-2022-24765 and Git 2.35.2's ownership-boundary hardening, including the new safe.directory exception mechanism; concrete evidence that ambient repository discovery could become an execution risk when configuration such as core.fsmonitor is read from an attacker-controlled repository.

title: gitformat-signature
book_use: Chapter 14: Git embeds detached cryptographic signatures in commits/tags and supports signed transactions; distinguishes a valid signature over a payload from broader claims about code safety or human understanding.

title: Artifact attestations
book_use: Chapter 14 and the Provenance Graph interlude: artifact attestations are cryptographically signed provenance claims that can bind a built artifact to repository, workflow, commit SHA, environment and triggering event; GitHub explicitly warns that attestations do not prove an artifact is secure, supporting the manuscript's evidence-layer model.

title: git-worktree
book_use: Chapter 15: multiple working trees can be attached to one repository and checked out independently; supports isolated task workspaces without claiming worktrees eliminate semantic conflicts.

title: Merging a pull request with a merge queue
book_use: Chapter 16 and the Branch Factory interlude: merge queues evaluate qualifying pull requests against the latest target branch and queued changes, illustrating integration as a stateful scheduling problem on busy branches.

title: Navigating code on GitHub
book_use: Chapter 17: GitHub derives symbol definitions and references for supported languages using tree-sitter-based code navigation; concrete example of semantic indexes layered above unchanged Git blobs.

title: git-diff
book_use: Chapter 17: rename and copy detection are diff-time similarity heuristics rather than permanent file identity; supports semantic interpretation as a derived view rather than stored truth.

title: Git 2.55
book_use: Chapters 4 and 18: Git 2.55 release commit dated June 29 2026 and signed off by Junio C Hamano.

title: Install / source release page
book_use: Current snapshot: git-scm.com lists Git 2.55.0 as the latest source release, released June 29 2026.

title: reftable
book_use: Chapters 18 and 19: documents reftable's planned Git 3.0 default status and scaling goals for large ref namespaces, including near-constant-time lookup and efficient atomic updates; includes Android and Rails examples.

title: partial-clone
book_use: Chapters 8 and 20: partial clone avoids eagerly downloading unneeded objects and can demand-fetch from promisor remotes; documents limitations and the shift away from complete eager local object possession.

title: gitprotocol-v2
book_use: Chapter 20: protocol v2 bundle-uri and promisor-remote capabilities; use for current mechanics and explicitly labeled future possibilities in the protocol text.

title: bundle-uri
book_use: Chapter 20: bundle URIs can bootstrap object databases before ordinary fetches and reduce load on origin servers or improve cloning over constrained links.

title: Scaling monorepo maintenance
source_type: Engineering article about upstream Git work
book_use: Chapter 8: multi-pack indexes, reachability bitmaps, and geometric repacking as concrete adaptations for very large repositories; note that the work described was contributed upstream to Git.

title: Git development repository
book_use: Current snapshot: main/master in late August 2026 contains release-note work for 2.56.0 while 2.55.0 remains the latest released source version; use development-branch facts only as unreleased state.

title: Git compatibility
book_use: Chapter 21: Jujutsu can use a regular Git repository backend, work with Git remotes and colocated workspaces, and layer a different user/change model over Git interoperability; supports replacement-by-overlay argument.

title: Sapling SCM and Git support modes
book_use: Chapter 21: Sapling emphasizes usability and monorepo scale, supports Git network interoperability and Git-backed modes while also pursuing different working-copy and storage machinery; supports layer-specific replacement argument.

title: Why Pijul?
book_use: Chapter 21: Pijul presents a patch/change-centered model with commuting independent changes and a different approach to conflicts and history; use as a conceptual alternative without claiming ecosystem dominance.

title: About migrations between GitHub products with GitHub Enterprise Importer
book_use: History Outside the Repository interlude: distinguishes Git source/history from separately migrated pull requests, issues, milestones, wikis, settings and other forge metadata; supports the two-histories argument.

title: git-notes
book_use: History Outside the Repository interlude: Git notes attach supplemental information to objects without changing the objects themselves and keep that commentary in separate notes refs with their own history.

title: Build Provenance v1.2
book_use: Provenance Graph interlude: defines provenance as verifiable information describing where, when and how an artifact was produced and models build definitions, run details and builder identity.

title: Working with agent sessions in the GitHub Copilot app
book_use: Branch Factory interlude: current agent tooling supports multiple isolated sessions simultaneously, each with its own branch/workspace, making parallel proposal production a present system behavior rather than a purely hypothetical forecast.

title: git-bundle
book_use: Long Archive interlude: bundles move objects and refs without a live server and can create full or incremental repository backups; supports offline possession and explicit prerequisite discussion.

title: Software Heritage persistent identifiers
book_use: Long Archive interlude: Software Heritage uses persistent identifiers for archived source artifacts and emphasizes content-derived identifiers that can be checked independently of the original forge location.

title: Takedown notices on mirrors
book_use: Long Archive interlude: preservation operates under legal and governance constraints; the archive and mirrors may need to evaluate legitimate takedown requests rather than treating permanence as an absolute technical rule.
